angle: angle 1 · a place and a time
title: What Life in a 1950s Factory Town Was Really Like

scenes.text: Five-thirty in the morning, nineteen fifty-five. It's still dark. In a thousand kitchens across town, a light comes on at the same moment. Coffee is percolating. Lunch pails are being packed. And down by the river, behind a chain-link fence, the smokestacks of the mill are already breathing white into the cold air.
scenes.caption: 5:30 IN THE MORNING

scenes.text: This is a factory town. One big employer, and everything else built around it. The steel mill, the paper mill, the auto plant, the glass works, the textile mill. In the nineteen fifties, millions of Americans lived in towns like this, from Pennsylvania to Michigan to the Carolinas.
scenes.caption: ONE TOWN, ONE EMPLOYER

scenes.text: Today we're going to spend one whole day there, from the first whistle in the morning to the last light in the tavern at night. The work, the houses, the families, the union hall and the ball field. This is what life in a nineteen fifties factory town was really like.
scenes.caption: ONE DAY IN A MILL TOWN

scenes.text: In the kitchen, mother packs the lunch pail. Two sandwiches, usually bologna or leftover meatloaf on white bread. An apple. A slice of pie wrapped in wax paper. And a thermos of hot coffee, clipped into the curved lid of a black metal pail that her husband has carried for fifteen years.
scenes.caption: THE LUNCH PAIL

scenes.text: Father eats standing up, in his work clothes. Heavy boots. Denim or canvas trousers. A flannel shirt, even in summer, because the sparks and the hot metal don't care what season it is. He kisses his wife, rubs the head of the youngest child still asleep at the table, and walks out the door.
scenes.caption: OUT THE DOOR

scenes.text: Most of the men walk to work. The houses were built close to the plant on purpose, decades earlier, often by the company itself. Rows of narrow frame houses on steep streets, with small front porches and backyards just big enough for a clothesline and a vegetable garden.
scenes.caption: THE COMPANY HOUSES

scenes.text: The streets fill with men walking in the same direction, lunch pails swinging, cigarettes glowing in the dark. Fathers, sons, brothers, neighbors. In a lot of families, three generations worked at the same plant. The grandfather on the pension, the father on the floor, and the son just hired on last spring.
scenes.caption: THREE GENERATIONS

scenes.text: At six forty-five the whistle blows, loud enough to hear all over town. Everybody in town sets their clocks by it. The men line up at the time clock, find their card in the rack, and punch in. One minute late is still late, and the foreman notices.
scenes.caption: THE WHISTLE

scenes.text: Inside, the noise is tremendous. Machines pounding. Furnaces roaring. Overhead cranes rumbling along their tracks. In a steel mill, the heat near the open hearth could make a man's face feel like it was on fire. The men talk with hand signals, or shout right into each other's ears.
scenes.caption: THE NOISE AND THE HEAT

scenes.text: It was hard work, and it could be dangerous work. Most men had a scar, a missing fingertip, or a story about the day a cable snapped. Safety rules existed, but they were looser than today. Hard hats and goggles were becoming common, but earplugs were rare, and many of those men grew hard of hearing by fifty.
scenes.caption: A DANGEROUS JOB

scenes.text: And yet, the men were proud of what they made. The steel in the new bridges. The glass in the windows of the new suburbs. The cars on every highway in America. When a man drove past a skyscraper or a dam, he could tell his children, our mill made the steel for that.
scenes.caption: WE MADE THAT

scenes.text: The foreman ran the floor. He was usually an older man who had come up through the ranks, worked every job in the plant, and knew every machine by its sound. He wore a white shirt instead of work clothes, and a different colored hard hat. Some foremen were feared. The good ones were respected for life.
scenes.caption: THE FOREMAN

scenes.text: At lunchtime, the whistle blows again. The men sit on crates and benches, open their pails, and trade sandwiches and stories. Who's sick. Who's getting married. Which foreman is in a bad mood. And always, always, how the high school team is going to do on Friday night.
scenes.caption: LUNCH AT THE MILL

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-five, about one in three American workers outside of agriculture belonged to a union. In factory towns, it was often nearly everybody on the plant floor. The union hall was down the street from the plant, with a flag out front and folding chairs inside.
scenes.caption: ONE IN THREE

scenes.text: The union negotiated the wages, the hours, the vacation and the pension. A contract might bring a raise of a few cents an hour, a week of paid vacation, and health insurance for the family. For a man whose own father had worked twelve-hour days for very little, those contracts felt like a miracle.
scenes.caption: THE CONTRACT

scenes.text: When contracts ran out and talks broke down, there were strikes. The men walked the picket line in shifts, carrying signs, keeping warm around barrels with fires burning inside. Wives brought coffee and sandwiches. Strikes could last weeks or months, and families lived on savings, strike pay and help from neighbors.
scenes.caption: THE PICKET LINE

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-five, the two biggest labor groups in the country, the A F of L and the C I O, merged into one. For the men on the plant floor, it was a sign of how powerful unions had become. Many of them would later say those were the best years for the American working man.
scenes.caption: 1955: THE MERGER

scenes.text: Wages in those plants were good for the time. A steelworker or an autoworker might earn around two dollars an hour in the mid-fifties, about twice the minimum wage. With overtime, a man could buy a house, a new car every few years, and a cottage on a lake for summer weekends.
scenes.caption: TWO DOLLARS AN HOUR

scenes.text: Everything in town depended on the plant. When the plant was busy, the stores on Main Street were busy. The car dealer sold new Chevrolets. The bakery sold birthday cakes. The bank gave out mortgages. When the plant laid men off, the whole town felt it within a week.
scenes.caption: WHEN THE PLANT WAS BUSY

scenes.text: On every corner, it seemed, there was a church and a tavern. The churches often belonged to the different groups who had come to work at the plant. Polish, Italian, Slovak, Irish, German, Black families who had come up from the South. Each had its own parish, its own festival and its own food.
scenes.caption: A CHURCH ON EVERY CORNER

scenes.text: The company was everywhere. It sponsored the Little League team and the bowling league. It built the community swimming pool, the library or the hospital wing. It held a picnic every summer, with games for the children and a hot dog for everybody. Some people loved the company. Some didn't. But nobody could ignore it.
scenes.caption: THE COMPANY PICNIC

scenes.text: Women ran the town while the men were at the plant. They shopped, cooked, cleaned, raised the children, ran the church suppers and the school bake sales. Some worked too, in the stores, the offices or the plant cafeteria. And many women in textile towns worked right on the mill floor, beside the men.
scenes.caption: THE WOMEN RAN THE TOWN

scenes.text: Children grew up with the sounds of the plant in their ears. The whistle. The trains rolling into the yard at night. The glow of the furnaces on the clouds after dark, which some children thought was the most beautiful thing in the world. They knew that someday, many of them would work there too.
scenes.caption: THE GLOW ON THE CLOUDS

scenes.text: There was a price for that glow. On some days the air smelled of sulfur, and the soot settled on windowsills and on the laundry hanging outside. Mothers wiped the porch railings every morning. Nobody talked much about pollution in nineteen fifty-five. People said it smelled like money, and they meant it.
scenes.caption: IT SMELLED LIKE MONEY

scenes.text: At three o'clock, the whistle blows for the end of the day shift. The gates open and the men pour out, tired and dirty, as the next shift walks in. The plant never stopped. Three shifts, around the clock, every day of the week except a few holidays a year.
scenes.caption: SHIFT CHANGE

scenes.text: Many of the men stopped at the tavern on the corner on the way home. One beer, sometimes two. A shot and a beer, if it had been a hard day. The bartender knew everybody's order. A ball game was on the radio, or on the small television above the bar, and the arguments about it never ended.
scenes.caption: ONE BEER ON THE WAY HOME

scenes.text: At home, dinner was on the table at five-thirty. Meat and potatoes, almost always. Pierogi on Friday in Polish homes, spaghetti on Sunday in Italian ones. The whole family sat down together, and the father got the biggest piece, because he had worked the hardest. Nobody argued about that.
scenes.caption: DINNER AT 5:30

scenes.text: After dinner, the men sat on the porch or worked in the garden. On summer evenings, the neighbors talked across the fences, and the children played in the street until dark. In the fall, the men went hunting on weekends. In the winter, there was the bowling league, the lodge, and church bingo.
scenes.caption: THE PORCH IN THE EVENING

scenes.text: The men on the night shift slept during the day, in bedrooms with heavy curtains, while the rest of the town went on outside. Their children learned to play quietly in the afternoons. Their wives learned to cook breakfast at three in the afternoon and dinner at midnight. In a factory town, every family lived on the plant's clock.
scenes.caption: THE NIGHT SHIFT FAMILY

scenes.text: Friday was payday and game day. The paychecks came out at the end of the shift, and that evening the stores stayed open late. Then the whole town went to the high school football stadium, which was often named after a company founder, and sat in the bleachers under the lights.
scenes.caption: PAYDAY AND GAME DAY

scenes.text: In mill towns, high school football was almost a religion. The players were the sons of the men in the bleachers. Many of them would be working beside their fathers within a year. And for a lot of those boys, Friday nights under the lights would be the best memory of their lives.
scenes.caption: ALMOST A RELIGION

scenes.text: After the game, the teenagers went to the drive-in or the diner. The parents went home, or to the social club for a dance. And late at night, the whistle blew for the shift change again, and a new crew of men walked through the gate, as the town slept.
scenes.caption: THE NIGHT SHIFT

scenes.text: The men who did those jobs were not famous. Nobody wrote songs about them, at least not then. But in nineteen fifty-five, America produced more steel, more cars and more goods than any country on earth. And it happened because of towns like this one, and the men and women who woke up at five-thirty every morning.
scenes.caption: NOT FAMOUS, BUT ESSENTIAL

scenes.text: For many of those towns, the good years didn't last. Starting in the late nineteen sixties and seventies, plants closed or moved away. Foreign competition, new technology and changing companies emptied out mills all over the country. The whistles went quiet. And the towns built around them had to find a way to survive.
scenes.caption: WHEN THE WHISTLE STOPPED

scenes.text: But if you grew up in a town like that, you remember it. The sound of the whistle. The smell of the mill when the wind changed. Your father's lunch pail on the kitchen counter. The pride in his voice when he said what his plant made. Those towns built America. And the people in them knew it.
scenes.caption: THOSE TOWNS BUILT AMERICA

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. Did your father or grandfather work at a mill or a plant? What did they make? We read every comment, and we'd love to hear their stories. Next, we're going to a wedding in nineteen sixty-five. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID YOUR FATHER MAKE?
